name: Fowler's syndrome
aliases: Primary disorder of urethral sphincter relaxation

clinicalPearls: Occurs in premenopausal women, typically presenting with painless complete urinary retention or obstructed voiding, a large-capacity bladder and characteristically reduced sensation of bladder fullness.
Strongly associated with polycystic ovaries and features of polycystic ovary syndrome, implying a hormonal influence on the urethral sphincter muscle.
Onset is often precipitated by an event such as surgery, childbirth or opioid analgesia.
The hallmark is abnormal striated urethral sphincter electromyography showing complex repetitive discharges and decelerating bursts, reflecting impaired sphincter relaxation.
Removal of an indwelling catheter is often difficult and uncomfortable because the sphincter grips the catheter.
Increased urethral sphincter volume on ultrasound and a raised maximum urethral closure pressure support the diagnosis.
Sacral neuromodulation is the most effective treatment and can restore spontaneous voiding.
The disorder is frequently and wrongly labelled as psychogenic retention, delaying appropriate care.
reference.pathophysiology: The primary abnormality is thought to lie within the striated (external) urethral sphincter itself, which fails to relax and instead maintains abnormal, ongoing electrical activity. Concentric needle electromyography reveals complex repetitive discharges and decelerating bursts, a pattern resembling a channelopathy that produces impaired relaxation and apparent sphincter muscle bulk; the strong association with polycystic ovaries suggests that sex steroids influence the stability of the sphincter muscle membrane. The continuously contracting sphincter generates a functional bladder outlet obstruction, but, crucially, the heightened afferent traffic arising from the abnormal sphincter is believed to inhibit the detrusor and suppress bladder sensation through spinal reflex pathways. This explains the characteristic paradox of a large-capacity, poorly sensate bladder that fails to empty, and provides the rationale for sacral neuromodulation, which is thought to restore normal afferent balance and permit voiding.
additionalDifferentials: Multiple sclerosis or other central neurological cause of retention
Cauda equina syndrome or a sacral cord lesion
Anatomical bladder outlet obstruction such as urethral stricture or stenosis
Pelvic mass causing extrinsic outlet compression
additionalInvestigations: Post-void residual measurement or bladder ultrasound
Concentric needle electromyography of the striated urethral sphincter
Ultrasound measurement of urethral sphincter volume
MRI of the spine and neuroaxis to exclude neurological disease
Pelvic ultrasound to assess for polycystic ovaries
redFlags: New neurological signs such as limb weakness, saddle anaesthesia or bowel dysfunction, suggesting a cord or cauda equina lesion
Upper urinary tract dilatation or deteriorating renal function
Fever or loin pain suggesting infection of a chronically retained or catheterised bladder
Rapidly progressive or bilateral lower limb symptoms
reference.prognosis: The condition is chronic, but sacral neuromodulation restores spontaneous voiding in a substantial proportion of women. Without effective treatment patients often remain dependent on catheterisation, which may be poorly tolerated.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosis as psychogenic retention, delaying appropriate treatment
Failure to perform striated sphincter electromyography
Assuming clean intermittent self-catheterisation will be well tolerated, when it is often painful because of the sphincter abnormality
Overlooking the association with polycystic ovaries
Attributing the retention solely to a precipitating event without recognising the underlying disorder
references: Neuro-urology and functional urology reference texts
International continence society terminology and standards documents
management: Offer sacral neuromodulation, which restores spontaneous voiding in a substantial proportion of women and is the definitive treatment
Manage bladder emptying in the interim with clean intermittent self-catheterisation, recognising it is often poorly tolerated because the sphincter grips the catheter
Avoid opioid analgesia, which can precipitate or worsen retention
Consider urethral sphincter botulinum toxin injection where neuromodulation is unsuitable or unsuccessful
Address the associated polycystic ovary syndrome
Monitor for urinary tract infection and safeguard the upper renal tracts and renal function
Refer to a specialist urology service and provide psychological support for this chronic condition
